note: Anything that makes a model fit noise or its evaluation instead of the signal: model, data and process causes, leakage, reuse of held-out data, named effects

aka: degrees of freedom in the analysis
answers.q: Gelman & Loken, after Borges: each reasonable analysis choice forks, and the path that fits your data looks principled in hindsight.
Give a model enough parameters and it can trace every training point, noise included, instead of the pattern.
Few examples leave many ways to fit them. The model picks one that works on those points and nowhere else.

aka: too many passes over the data
answers.q: Past some point the model stops learning the pattern and starts memorizing the noise. Validation loss turns upward.
Nothing penalizes wild weights or jagged fits, so the model is free to chase every noisy point.
A model can't tell signal from noise, so it fits both, and the noise doesn't repeat on new data.

aka: overlap between train and test sets
test set in the training data
test data in the training set
answers.q: Not true overfitting, but the same hangover: test information leaks into training, the score soars, and production disappoints.
In high dimensions, data is sparse and some meaningless rule will separate any training set. Bellman coined it in 1957.
Early stopping halts when validation loss turns up. Skip it and you train straight past the best point.
Dropout stops neurons co-adapting by randomly silencing them. Without it, units can team up to memorize.

aka: number of features exceeds number of samples
bag of words with a huge vocabulary
answers.q: With more features than samples, some combination will explain the training labels perfectly by pure chance.
Each extra layer adds capacity to carve up the input space. Stack enough on a small dataset and the net memorizes it.
Wide hidden layers hold enough units to memorize the training set one example at a time.

aka: using the test set for tuning
hyperparameter tuning on the test set
model selection on the test set
error analysis on the test set
early stopping on the test set
checkpoint selection on the test set
picking the best epoch on the test set
using test data for model selection
answers.q: Every look at the test set trains you on it. Once you tune against it, it is just another validation set.
An unpruned tree splits until every leaf is pure, so each leaf can end up holding a single training point.

aka: fitting a polynomial of degree n-1
answers.q: Fit N points with a degree N-1 polynomial and you get a perfect fit that swings wildly between them. Bishop's classic picture.
A sample that misses the real world's variety teaches rules that only hold inside the sample.
Without flips, crops and noise, the model sees each example in one form only and can memorize exactly that form.
Zhang et al. 2017: standard nets fit even randomly shuffled labels perfectly. The capacity to memorize is the whole problem.
Weight decay shrinks weights toward zero every step. Skip it and weights can grow large enough to bend sharply around single points.

aka: too many trees in gradient boosting
answers.q: Each round chases the remaining residuals, and eventually those are mostly noise. Early stopping on validation is the fix.
One lucky split can flatter any model. Cross-validation averages over several, so a fluke is harder to mistake for skill.
Barz & Denzler 2019: 3.3% of CIFAR-10 and 10% of CIFAR-100 test images have duplicates in the training set.
Features with no signal still give the model more ways to fit noise. Any random column can 'explain' a few training points.
With k=1 every training point is its own nearest neighbor, so training error is zero and the boundary bends around every outlier.

aka: using training error as the metric
answers.q: With no held-out data, training accuracy is the only signal, and it only goes up. Overfitting stays invisible until deployment.

aka: few examples of the minority class
answers.q: A rare class has few examples, so the model memorizes those few instead of learning what the class looks like.
Huskies on snow, cows on grass: the model learns the background. Sagawa et al. 2020: overparameterization can make it worse.
In Bishop's polynomial example, the overfit M=9 curve has coefficients in the hundreds of thousands. Penalties tame them.
One extreme point can drag a flexible fit toward it, especially under squared error.

aka: using the label as a feature
answers.q: A feature secretly computed from the answer gives a perfect fit and zero value once the answer is unknown.

aka: repeated use of the validation set
answers.q: Each peek at a holdout leaks a few bits. Dwork et al.'s reusable holdout (Thresholdout) adds noise to answers to cap the damage.

aka: test set reuse across the community
answers.q: Thousands of submissions tuned against one public score, then the private leaderboard reshuffles everyone. Shake-up day.

aka: selecting features on the full dataset
selecting features using all the data
feature selection on the whole dataset
selecting features before the train test split
answers.q: ESL's classic trap: pick the 'best' genes using all labels, then cross-validate, and pure noise scores far above chance.

aka: fitting the scaler on all data
fitting preprocessing on the test set
answers.q: Test-set statistics seep into training through the scaler, imputer or PCA. Fit on train, only transform test.
Train on Tuesday to predict Monday and the backtest looks gorgeous. Split time series by time, not at random.

aka: same patient in train and test
same user in train and test
same subject in train and test
same person in train and test
same speaker in train and test
patches from the same image in train and test
answers.q: If one patient has several scans, a random split puts them on both sides. The model learns people, not disease.
Slice, subset and retest until p dips under 0.05. Run enough comparisons and noise will oblige.
Bennett et al. 2009 found 'brain activity' in a dead salmon by skipping the correction. Ig Nobel Prize, 2012.
A few hundred validation examples give noisy scores. Pick the best of many configurations and you mostly pick the luckiest.

aka: validation set differs from test set
answers.q: If validation doesn't look like the test or the real world, you tune the model toward the wrong target.
Fit the training distribution too closely and a different test distribution exposes every quirk you learned.

aka: full fine-tuning on a tiny dataset
fine-tuning a huge model on few examples
fine-tuning large model on small dataset
transfer learning with too little data
answers.q: Billions of parameters and a few hundred examples: after a couple of epochs the model simply recites the training set.

aka: training from scratch on small data
training from scratch on a small dataset
answers.q: Without pretrained features, a big model must learn everything from a small dataset, and memorizing it is the easiest route.

aka: benchmark data in the training set
answers.q: Benchmark questions scraped into web-scale pretraining data: the model looks brilliant because it studied the exam.

aka: architecture not suited to the data
answers.q: A fully connected net on images must learn translation invariance from scratch, so it memorizes pixels. Convolutions bake it in.
Keskar et al. 2017: large batches tend to land in sharp minima, which generalize worse than the flat ones small batches find.

aka: model just big enough to fit the data
number of parameters equals number of samples
answers.q: Belkin et al. 2019: test error peaks when a model is just big enough to fit the training set exactly, then falls again beyond it.
Random oversampling copies minority examples, so the model sees the same few points over and over and memorizes them.
Blum & Hardt: submit random label vectors, keep those scoring above chance, majority-vote them. Great public score, zero skill.

aka: picking the best of many models
selecting the best of many runs
answers.q: Pick the best of many noisy scores and the winner's number is inflated: part of its lead was luck.
Picard 2021, 'torch.manual_seed(3407) is all you need': seeds alone move scores. Pick the best on the test set and you overfit.

aka: hypothesizing after the results are known
answers.q: Kerr 1998: run the experiment, find something, then write the introduction as if you predicted it.
Try enough trading rules on one price history and one will look brilliant. Bailey et al. quantified the odds.

aka: tuning and evaluating on the same CV folds
tuning and evaluating on the same folds
same CV for tuning and evaluation
hyperparameter tuning inside the evaluation folds
using the same cross-validation for model selection and evaluation
answers.q: Cawley & Talbot 2010: the CV score you tuned on is optimistically biased. Nest an outer loop to evaluate.
Check the p-value after every batch and stop when it dips below 0.05, and your false-positive rate balloons far past 5%.

aka: adjacent frames in train and test
video frames in both train and test
answers.q: Overlapping windows or neighboring video frames put near-copies on both sides of the split, so the test score only measures memory.
Near-duplicate predictors make coefficients unstable: tiny noise swings them wildly in opposite directions.
Each add-or-drop step picks whatever fits this sample best, so fit and p-values come out flattering even for pure noise.

aka: augmented copies in train and test
answers.q: Copies or synthetic neighbors of one sample land on both sides of the split, so the test set is full of near-twins of training data.
Encode a category by its mean label over the same rows and each row carries its own answer. CatBoost's ordered statistics avoid it.

aka: using the index as a feature
answers.q: An ID or a 50,000-level category lets the model memorize one row per value: perfect training fit, zero generalization.
The meta-learner sees base-model predictions made on rows they trained on. Those are far too good, so it trusts them blindly.
Train on your own guesses and the wrong ones get reinforced. Arazo et al. 2020 named it confirmation bias and fought it with mixup.

aka: optimizing a proxy objective too hard
answers.q: Gao et al. 2022: push a policy hard against a reward model and the proxy score climbs while the true score falls.

aka: too many epochs of adversarial training
answers.q: Rice et al. 2020: in adversarial training, robust test error bottoms out early, then climbs while robust training error keeps falling.
Cobbe et al. 2019 (CoinRun): RL agents trained on too few levels memorize them and stumble on new ones.

aka: too many gradient updates per step
answers.q: Nikishin et al. 2022: deep RL agents overfit their earliest experiences and never recover. Periodic resets of layers help.

Different labs, scanners or hospitals leave fingerprints. If labels correlate with site, the model learns the site, not the biology.
Maximum likelihood trusts the sample completely. A Gaussian prior (MAP) is just L2 regularization in Bayesian clothes.
Most 5-grams in new text never appeared in training. A high-order n-gram model memorizes sequences, hence smoothing.
Each hand-made interaction is another degree of freedom. Try thousands and some will fit noise by chance.
A kernel or smoother so narrow that each point listens only to itself. The fit interpolates every wiggle of the noise.
Large C punishes every margin violation, so the SVM contorts its boundary around noisy points. Small C is the stronger regularizer.
A factorization with too many latent factors can reproduce the observed ratings exactly and predict unseen ones poorly.
Give an autoencoder a hidden layer wider than its input and with no regularizer it can just copy the input through, learning nothing.
File names, timestamps, folder paths or row order: if they correlate with the label, the model reads them instead of the content.

aka: multiple epochs on the same data
answers.q: Muennighoff et al. 2023: LLMs can repeat a corpus for about 4 epochs with little loss, but returns collapse far beyond that.
A lone flexible model is high-variance: its fit swings with the sample. Averaging many models (bagging) cancels much of that swing.
More unknowns than equations: infinitely many exact fits exist, and nothing says the one you got is the right one.

aka: same annotators in train and test
answers.q: Geva et al. 2019: models do better on test examples from annotators who also wrote the training data. They learn the writer, not the task.

aka: training CTR models for multiple epochs
answers.q: Zhou et al. 2022: large click-through-rate models do fine in epoch one, then test AUC drops sharply when epoch two begins.
Train on rendered or generated data and the model learns the generator's quirks, which the real world doesn't share.
Fitting many kernel hyperparameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood can overfit: Lotfi et al. 2022 explain when it fails.
de Haan et al. 2019: a driving policy watches the brake light, not the pedestrian. More inputs can make imitation worse.

aka: training a GAN on little data
answers.q: Karras et al. 2020: on small datasets the GAN's discriminator memorizes the real images. Their fix: adaptive discriminator augmentation.
One-hot targets reward ever-larger logits, so the net grows overconfident on training points. Label smoothing caps the target.

Each extra lag adds a parameter. With a short series, a high-order autoregression fits the sample's noise.
Likelihood never decreases as you add mixture components. At one per point, the model has memorized the data.
